title: Wilderness Navigation: Topographic Maps, Bearings, and Route Planning
learner_summary: A recreational hiker can identify basic topographic-map symbols and has used marked trails, but is new to systematic off-trail navigation. They can read a compass dial and estimate distances but sometimes confuse map north, magnetic north, and the direction of a back bearing. The next lesson should build on map-reading basics without assuming experience navigating in poor visibility.

objectives.text: Interpret map scales, contour lines, and basic compass directions on a topographic map.
Take, adjust, and follow a map-derived bearing using a compass, including back bearings and checks against terrain.
Plan a short off-trail route using handrails, catching features, checkpoints, and conservative turnaround criteria.

facts.text: A bearing is a clockwise angle measured from a stated north reference; a grid or true bearing and a magnetic bearing are not automatically interchangeable.
A map-to-terrain bearing can be measured by aligning a compass edge with the intended route on the map and orienting the compass housing to the map north reference before accounting for declination.
Magnetic declination is the local angular difference between magnetic north and true north, and the correct adjustment depends on the map north reference and the sign of the local declination.
In a region with 10 degrees east magnetic declination, a 100-degree true bearing corresponds to a 90-degree magnetic bearing, assuming no additional compass correction.
The reciprocal or back bearing is 180 degrees from the outward bearing: add 180 degrees if the bearing is below 180 degrees, otherwise subtract 180 degrees.
To follow a bearing, orient the compass to the desired magnetic heading, select a visible object on that line, travel to it, and repeat rather than watching the compass continuously while walking.
A compass heading should be cross-checked with identifiable terrain or checkpoints; a single bearing alone does not establish an exact position.

misconceptions.text: A 1:100,000 map shows more local detail than a 1:24,000 map.
misconceptions.correction: At the same physical map size, 1:24,000 is the larger-scale map and generally shows more local detail.

misconceptions.text: Closely spaced contour lines indicate a gentle slope.
misconceptions.correction: For a fixed contour interval, closer contour spacing indicates a steeper slope.

misconceptions.text: To return along a straight route, keep the original bearing unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: The return direction is the reciprocal bearing, 180 degrees opposite the outward bearing.

misconceptions.text: Contour-line V shapes in a stream valley usually point downhill.
misconceptions.correction: Where contours cross an ordinary stream valley, the V generally points upstream, toward higher elevation.

misconceptions.text: The north end of a magnetic compass needle always points to true north.
misconceptions.correction: The needle aligns approximately with the local magnetic field; magnetic declination must be considered when translating between true and magnetic bearings.

misconceptions.text: If one landform matches the map, the hiker has identified their exact location.
misconceptions.correction: A single landform or bearing rarely establishes a unique position; use multiple independent landmarks and terrain checks.

misconceptions.text: Once a bearing is chosen, the hiker should walk while staring at the compass dial.
misconceptions.correction: Sight a stable point along the bearing, walk to it while attending to footing and surroundings, then repeat and verify against terrain.
